title: Imtiaz Ali Made a Partition Love Story. The First Reviews Say It's His Best Work in Years.
excerpt: Main Vaapas Aaunga reunites the Chamkila duo, adds AR Rahman and Naseeruddin Shah, and already has Kabir Khan in tears. This Thursday.
body:
The first people to see Main Vaapas Aaunga walked out of the screening room looking slightly broken. In the best possible way.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=PRUTWluKRW8

Imtiaz Ali's new film — a sprawling, two-timeline love story set against the Partition of 1947 — held a special screening in Mumbai this week, and the reactions are the kind filmmakers dream about but rarely get. Not polite applause. Not "it was nice." The kind where people reach for words and keep circling back to the same one: moving.

Kabir Khan, a filmmaker who knows a thing or two about emotionally charged storytelling, called it "a very moving film" and added, with noticeable weight, "It's still very relevant because of the world that we're living in today." He described it as "such a multilayered film" — and then admitted he needed to sleep on it before he could fully process what he'd watched.

Sunidhi Chauhan, who's been in enough Bollywood screening rooms to know when the energy is real, kept it simple: "All I can say is it's beautiful."

And Aaliyah Kashyap — who watched it twice — called it "a beautiful and hard-hitting story with powerful performances and amazing music." She came back for seconds. That tells you something.

Even Ektaa Kapoor went lyrical: "Emotional, timeless, and stays with you long after it ends."

The Dream Team Nobody Expected

The film reunites Imtiaz Ali with Diljit Dosanjh, whose collaboration on Amar Singh Chamkila reminded everyone that Diljit isn't just a concert-selling, Wembley-announcing machine — he's a proper actor when the material demands it. Here, the material is demanding plenty.

Alongside Diljit, the cast reads like someone raided every generation of Indian talent at once. Naseeruddin Shah anchors one end, bringing decades of screen gravitas to a role that reportedly bridges both timelines. Vedang Raina — The Archies' breakout star, now rapidly proving that wasn't a fluke — plays Keenu, a young man caught between eras and identities. And Sharvari, who's about to become inescapable between this and the upcoming Alpha, plays Jiya.

The film unfolds across two worlds: the chaos and heartbreak of 1947, and the present day, where the echoes of Partition still shape how people love, lose, and find their way home. It's Imtiaz Ali territory — longing, distance, the ache of belonging — but filtered through history rather than highway road trips. The dual-timeline structure means Diljit and Naseeruddin Shah carry the emotional weight across generations, while Vedang and Sharvari anchor the love story that threads through it all.

AR Rahman at the Border

If you needed proof that the film carries real emotional weight, look at what happened at the Attari Border last week. AR Rahman — who composed the film's score with lyrics by the great Irshad Kamil — performed a full concert at the India-Pakistan border crossing for BSF jawans, with the film's cast in attendance.

The setlist included songs from the film: Maskara (performed by Nilanjana Ghosh and Vedang Raina himself), Ishq Mastana (by the great Mohit Chauhan), and the soaring Chanda Suraj Lakhon Taare. Then Rahman closed with Maa Tujhe Salaam, because of course he did. At the actual border. With soldiers in the audience. The man understands the assignment.

Imtiaz Ali, rarely one for grand statements, said something at the event that feels like the film's thesis: "Not only homes and lives were lost, but hearts were broken as well. We bring a message of love because, ultimately, only love sustains us."

For the Diaspora, This One Hits Different

Here's the thing about a Partition film releasing in 2026: for millions of Indians in the US, UK, and Canada, Partition isn't ancient history. It's the story grandparents carry in their bones. It's the house in Lahore or Rawalpindi nobody can go back to. It's the reason some families ended up in Southall or Jackson Heights instead of the towns they were born in.

Imtiaz Ali isn't making a documentary. He's making a love story. But love stories set against Partition have a way of unlocking something primal in diaspora audiences — the longing that's always there, always just under the surface, always waiting for someone to give it a melody. And with AR Rahman composing that melody, the odds are very much in this film's favour.

"This is such a unique event. AR Rahman performing at the Attari Gate. This performance is an ode to the national spirit, to our bravehearts on the border, the BSF and the Indian Army, and to the spirit of solidarity and love that binds us all." — Imtiaz Ali

Main Vaapas Aaunga arrives in theatres worldwide on June 12. Produced by Birla Studios, Applause Entertainment, and Window Seat Films, with music on Tips Music. The title translates to "I Will Come Back." Given what the first audiences are saying, you might want to come back for a second watch, too.
